text: Hello and welcome to the next part of the data engineering zoom camp in module two.
Now today we're going to be looking specifically at how you can orchestrate Python code inside of
Kestra. Now while we won't be necessarily orchestrating Python code in the ETL pipelines will be
building in the next part, this is still a fundamental part of data engineering and you might want
to use this in your project later on. So let's cover it today. Now the Python script we're going to
be using today is available inside of the GitHub repository. So I'd recommend checking that out.
It's called O2 underscore Python. We can copy and paste this into Kestra and we'll see a workflow
that looks a little bit like this. Now this workflow just has one task in it. It's got the Python
script task. Now there are actually a couple of ways you can run Python inside a Kestra. We're
going to be using the script task today, which allows you to write your Python code directly inside
of the workflow. So you can see here under this script property, we've written the Python code
directly in the workflow. Now this is great for small snippets of Python where you just need to be
able to manipulate a small bit of data and you want to be able to just tap into the power of Python
to do so. But maybe you've got a bigger project that you've written the Python code locally outside
of Kestra and you want to be able to just execute those files. Now that's where the command task comes
in. This task allows you to take a file and then be able to execute it using the command task. We
can upload these files as namespace files where we can then access them inside of our workflow.
And as you can see here, we've just included the permission to allow it to access namespace files
and then we can just execute the command just like we would in our terminal on our local machine.
Now it's also worth clarifying that the way that Python works inside of Kestra is by default,
it's going to spin up a Docker container to run that code. This is great because it means that
any dependencies it needs to use in this case, requests and Kestra, which for context use UV
under the hood to manage those dependencies. It's going to install those inside of a container,
you can specify the versions you need and it's not going to clash with any other workflows or even
other tasks you have in that workflow that are also using Python. Now you can also specify the
container image it's going to use. So maybe you've got a pre-built image that contains a lot of
these dependencies that you need. So you can build that image, have that hosted in a registry,
and then access it directly here. So this means that your task runner, which in this case is Docker,
will build using that image. It's got the dependencies it needs and it can just execute your code.
Now there are options to run in other task runners, the most notable being process where you can
execute it as a sub process on the machine of Kestra. Now in our case, because Kestra is running in
a Docker container, it will just run it inside that Kestra container. But if you were running Kestra
as a local executable, it will just run it as a sub process there. So that's where maybe having
a virtual environment would be a good idea because it will access any existing dependencies on your
system. And so you might want to be able to just put it in a virtual environment and control
their dependencies a little more. But we don't need to do that when we're using a container because
that gives us the isolation we need. Now just like any other Python code, this code here is just
written directly inside. There's nothing special about it. But we are using the Kestra library that
allows us to then be able to send data generated in the Python code back to Kestra as an output.
So you'll see here we've got this Kestra library here. We're doing dot outputs and we're passing
it a JSON effectively on this case, a dictionary with key value pairs. If I execute this workflow
now, we'll see it's going to spin up a container and it's going to install those dependencies using
UV. And then once it's finished, it's going to destroy that container. And if we go to outputs,
we can see it was able to send us an output called downloads with that number. And we can then
access that later on in future tasks if we want to. So that gives you an overview of how Python works
inside of Kestra. You can obviously take this a step further by using a Git plugin to automatically
pull your code to your workflow, have Kestra then be able to execute those files from that code,
and then generate data that you can then pass on to other tasks. Hopefully you found that useful.
In the next part of the course, we're going to start looking at actually building a data pipeline.
So definitely stay tuned for that.
